s: A 22-year-old woman has mucopurulent cervical discharge. A vaginal swab nucleic acid amplification test is positive. In cell culture, the organism forms glycogen-rich cytoplasmic inclusions that stain with iodine, and it cannot synthesize its own ATP.
l: Which form of this organism attaches to and enters new host cells?
e: The organism is *Chlamydia trachomatis*, an obligate intracellular bacterium with a two-form life cycle. The small, metabolically inactive **elementary body** is the infectious particle: it survives outside cells, binds columnar epithelium and enters by endocytosis. Inside the vacuole it converts to the reticulate body, which divides by binary fission and fills the glycogen-rich inclusion before reorganizing into new elementary bodies that are released. The reticulate body replicates but is too fragile to infect, and endospores, pseudohyphae and trophozoites belong to other kinds of organisms entirely.

w.Reticulate body: The reticulate body is the larger form that divides by binary fission inside the vacuole; it is fragile outside the cell and cannot start a new infection.
w.Endospore: Endospores are the dormant, heat-resistant forms of gram-positive rods such as Clostridium and Bacillus; chlamydiae have no spore stage at all.
w.Pseudohypha: Pseudohyphae are chains of elongated budding yeast, the tissue form of Candida seen on a KOH preparation of vaginal discharge, not a bacterial form.
w.Trophozoite: Trophozoites are the motile feeding stage of protozoa such as Trichomonas vaginalis, which appear as flagellated cells moving on a saline wet mount.

et: Invades tissue as chains of yeast
bl: Chlamydia's infectious form is the elementary body; the reticulate body replicates inside the inclusion but cannot infect.

s: A 24-year-old man comes to the clinic because of dysuria and a thick yellow urethral discharge for 3 days. He had the same illness 1 year ago and was treated. Temperature is 37.2°C. Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils. The organism grows on Thayer-Martin agar, is oxidase-positive and ferments glucose but not maltose.
l: Which property of this organism best explains why his earlier infection did not protect him?
e: This is gonococcal urethritis. *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* keeps recombining its pilin genes, so the pili that mediate attachment keep changing their antigens. Antibodies made during the first infection no longer recognize the new pili, which is why reinfection is common and why no vaccine exists. IgA protease and lipooligosaccharide are real gonococcal virulence factors, but they explain mucosal survival and inflammation rather than failed immunity. The gonococcus lacks a polysaccharide capsule, unlike the meningococcus, and it grows on agar, unlike obligate intracellular chlamydia.

w.A polysaccharide capsule: The meningococcus, not the gonococcus, carries a polysaccharide capsule, which is why meningococcal vaccines exist while gonococcal vaccines do not.
w.IgA protease secretion: IgA protease cleaves secretory IgA on the mucosa and helps colonization, but it does not change the surface antigens that memory recognizes after recovery.
w.Lipooligosaccharide endotoxin: Lipooligosaccharide drives the intense neutrophil response and the purulent discharge, yet antibody against an unchanged molecule would still recognize a second infection.
w.Obligate intracellular growth: Obligate intracellular growth describes chlamydia, which cannot make ATP; this organism grows on Thayer-Martin agar, so it is not confined to host cells.

et: Capsule antibodies protect; basis of vaccines
bl: Gonococcal pili undergo antigenic variation, so a prior infection leaves no protective immunity and no vaccine exists.

s: A 19-year-old woman has had fever and pain in her wrists and hands for 3 days. Examination shows swelling and tenderness along the extensor tendon sheaths of both wrists and four small pustules on an erythematous base on her forearms and ankles. Three years ago she was hospitalized for meningococcal meningitis. Blood cultures grow gram-negative diplococci that ferment glucose but not maltose.
l: Deficiency of which of the following most likely predisposes her to these infections?
e: Tenosynovitis, sparse pustules and polyarthralgia are **disseminated gonococcal infection**, and she has also had meningococcal disease. Recurrent or disseminated Neisseria infections point to a deficiency of the terminal complement components, C5 through C9, which assemble the membrane attack complex that kills these thin-walled bacteria in blood. C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, NADPH oxidase deficiency causes infections with catalase-positive organisms, CD18 deficiency causes leukocyte adhesion failure with delayed umbilical cord separation, and Bruton tyrosine kinase deficiency removes B cells.

w.C1 esterase inhibitor: Loss of C1 esterase inhibitor lets bradykinin accumulate, causing hereditary angioedema with facial and airway swelling rather than bloodstream Neisseria infections.
w.NADPH oxidase: NADPH oxidase deficiency is chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent infections by catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus.
w.CD18 integrin: CD18 deficiency is leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, marked by delayed umbilical cord separation, neutrophilia and skin infections that form no pus.
w.Bruton tyrosine kinase: Bruton tyrosine kinase deficiency blocks B-cell maturation, so boys develop recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria once maternal antibody wanes.

et: Episodic swelling of face and airway
bl: Recurrent or disseminated Neisseria infections suggest terminal complement C5–C9 deficiency, because the membrane attack complex kills Neisseria.

s: A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of sharp right upper quadrant pain for 2 days that worsens with deep breathing. She has had dull lower abdominal pain and vaginal discharge for 1 week. She has a new sexual partner and does not use condoms. Temperature is 38.4°C. There is tenderness below the right costal margin. Pelvic examination shows mucopurulent cervical discharge, pain when the cervix is moved and bilateral adnexal tenderness. Urine hCG is negative. Serum aminotransferases are normal, and ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder without stones or wall thickening.
l: Which of the following best explains her right upper quadrant pain?
e: Cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness establish pelvic inflammatory disease. Organisms can track up the right paracolic gutter and inflame the **liver capsule**, a perihepatitis called Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, which hurts with breathing because the capsule moves against the diaphragm. The liver parenchyma is spared, so aminotransferases stay normal, and the capsule later scars to the abdominal wall with violin-string adhesions. Acute cholecystitis is the classic competing diagnosis, but a normal gallbladder on ultrasound argues strongly against it. Viral hepatitis would raise aminotransferases, and pneumonia and pyelonephritis do not explain the pelvic findings. She needs the PID regimen.

w.Acute cholecystitis: Cholecystitis also causes right upper quadrant pain and fever, but ultrasound would show stones or a thickened wall, and gallbladder disease cannot explain her pelvic findings.
w.Acute viral hepatitis: Hepatitis inflames the liver parenchyma and raises aminotransferases into the hundreds or thousands; hers are normal because only the capsule is involved.
w.Right lower lobe pneumonia: Lower lobe pneumonia can cause pleuritic upper abdominal pain, but it brings cough and crackles and would not account for cervical discharge and adnexal tenderness.
w.Acute pyelonephritis: Pyelonephritis causes fever with flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness, usually with pyuria; pain on moving the cervix points to the genital tract instead.

bl: Right upper quadrant pain with PID signs and a normal gallbladder is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis inflammation of the liver capsule, treated with the PID regimen.

pt.say: Look at step 6, where the dashed path climbs the right gutter to the liver capsule: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis inflames the capsule, not the gallbladder or the liver cells.

s: A 20-year-old woman has had lower abdominal pain and fever for 2 days. Temperature is 38.1°C. Pelvic examination shows purulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness without a mass. Urine hCG is negative. Transvaginal ultrasound shows no abscess. She is tolerating oral fluids, has no drug allergies and will be treated as an outpatient.
o: Ceftriaxone IM once, then doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
Azithromycin orally once, then metronidazole alone for 7 days
Ceftriaxone IM once as a single dose with no oral follow-up
Doxycycline alone for 7 days, without a cephalosporin
Oral metronidazole for 7 days, then retesting in 3 months
e: This is outpatient pelvic inflammatory disease, a polymicrobial upper-tract infection started by gonorrhea or chlamydia and joined by anaerobes. The CDC 2021 regimen covers all three: **ceftriaxone** 500 mg IM once for the gonococcus, then 14 days of doxycycline for chlamydia and metronidazole for anaerobes. Treatment starts on clinical grounds because delay increases tubal scarring. A single ceftriaxone dose treats uncomplicated gonorrhea but leaves chlamydia and anaerobes untreated. Doxycycline alone misses the gonococcus, and metronidazole alone treats only anaerobes and trichomonas.

w.Azithromycin orally once, then metronida: A single azithromycin dose is too brief for upper-tract chlamydial infection and gives unreliable gonococcal coverage, and a 7-day metronidazole course is bacterial vaginosis therapy.
w.Ceftriaxone IM once as a single dose wit: One ceftriaxone dose cures uncomplicated gonorrhea, but pelvic infection also involves chlamydia and anaerobes that need two weeks of doxycycline and metronidazole.
w.Doxycycline alone for 7 days, without a: Doxycycline covers chlamydia, but gonococci resist tetracyclines, and a 7-day course is the cervicitis regimen, too short for tubal infection.
w.Oral metronidazole for 7 days, then rete: Metronidazole treats anaerobes, trichomonas and bacterial vaginosis; alone it leaves the gonococcus and chlamydia that started the infection untouched.

et: Ceftriaxone IM once, then doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
Azithromycin orally once, then metronidazole alone for 7 days
Too short for the upper tract
Ceftriaxone IM once as a single dose with no oral follow-up
Doxycycline alone for 7 days, without a cephalosporin
Oral metronidazole for 7 days, then retesting in 3 months
bl: Outpatient PID needs ceftriaxone IM once plus 14 days of doxycycline and metronidazole to cover gonococcus, chlamydia and anaerobes.

s: A 28-year-old man comes to the clinic 5 days after returning from a trip abroad because of two painful penile sores. Examination shows two deep ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and a gray-yellow purulent base, and a single tender, fluctuant left inguinal lymph node. Gram stain of ulcer material shows small gram-negative rods arranged in parallel chains.
l: Which organism is the most likely cause?
e: Painful, ragged ulcers with a purulent base plus a tender, suppurating node on one side are chancroid, caused by *Haemophilus ducreyi*, a small gram-negative rod that lines up in parallel chains, the school-of-fish pattern. It is uncommon in the United States and often acquired abroad; treatment is one dose of azithromycin or ceftriaxone. Herpes simplex also causes painful ulcers, but they begin as grouped vesicles, are shallow and show no bacteria. The syphilis chancre and the ulcers of Klebsiella granulomatis and lymphogranuloma venereum are painless.

w.Treponema pallidum: The syphilis chancre is a single painless, indurated ulcer with a clean base, and its nodes are rubbery and nontender, the opposite of this purulent picture.
w.Klebsiella granulomatis: Donovanosis causes a painless, beefy-red ulcer that bleeds easily, with Donovan bodies inside macrophages and no true suppurative node.
w.Chlamydia trachomatis serovar L2: Lymphogranuloma venereum begins with a tiny painless ulcer that usually goes unnoticed; buboes come weeks later, and chlamydiae are not seen on Gram stain.
w.Herpes simplex virus type 2: Genital herpes causes grouped vesicles that become shallow ulcers with tender bilateral nodes; Gram stain shows no bacteria, and PCR would detect viral DNA.

et: NAAT; not seen on Gram stain
bl: Painful ragged ulcers with a suppurating node and school-of-fish gram-negative rods mean chancroid from Haemophilus ducreyi.

pt.say: Look at the painful-ulcer rows: Haemophilus ducreyi gives a deep ragged ulcer, a painful node that suppurates and school-of-fish rods on Gram stain.

s: A 30-year-old man who has sex with men comes to the clinic because of painful swelling in his left groin for 10 days. Three weeks ago he noticed a small painless sore on his penis that healed within a few days. Temperature is 38.0°C. Examination shows tender, matted inguinal lymph nodes above and below the inguinal ligament, with a draining sinus. A nucleic acid amplification test of the node aspirate is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis.
l: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
e: A fleeting painless ulcer followed by painful, matted inguinal buboes with the groove sign is **lymphogranuloma venereum**, caused by the invasive L1 to L3 serovars of *Chlamydia trachomatis*. Because these serovars spread through lymphatics and cause deep tissue infection, treatment is doxycycline for 21 days, three times the course for uncomplicated genital chlamydia. Benzathine penicillin treats syphilis but has no activity against chlamydiae, which lack classic peptidoglycan. Acyclovir treats herpes, ceftriaxone treats gonorrhea, and metronidazole treats trichomonas and anaerobes.

w.Benzathine penicillin G once: Benzathine penicillin cures early syphilis, whose chancre is also painless, but beta-lactams do not work against chlamydiae because their wall has almost no peptidoglycan.
w.Acyclovir for 10 days: Acyclovir treats a first episode of genital herpes, which causes painful grouped vesicles rather than a painless sore followed by suppurating buboes.
w.Ceftriaxone IM once: Ceftriaxone is the single-dose treatment for gonorrhea; it does not reliably eradicate chlamydia, which the amplification test has already identified here.
w.Metronidazole for 7 days: Metronidazole treats trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis and the anaerobes of pelvic infection; it has no activity against obligate intracellular chlamydiae.

bl: Lymphogranuloma venereum from Chlamydia L1 to L3 is treated with doxycycline for 21 days, longer than for genital chlamydia.

pt.say: Find the LGV row: a small ulcer that heals fast, then painful buboes with the groove sign, treated with doxycycline for 21 days.

s: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has her first prenatal visit at 10 weeks' gestation. She has had two previous miscarriages and a deep venous thrombosis. She has no genital lesions or rash. Routine screening shows a reactive RPR at a titer of 1:4. A Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA) test is negative.
l: Which of the following best explains the reactive RPR?
e: The RPR detects antibody against **cardiolipin**, a phospholipid, so the antiphospholipid antibodies of lupus react in the test and produce a biologic false positive, usually at a low titer. Her miscarriages and thrombosis suggest antiphospholipid syndrome. The negative treponemal test settles it, because TP-PA detects antibody against the organism itself and is positive in every stage of true syphilis beyond the first days. Past treated syphilis gives the opposite pattern, and late latent syphilis would also have a reactive treponemal test. The prozone effect causes a falsely negative RPR, not a false positive.

w.Early primary syphilis: In very early primary syphilis both tests can be negative, but treponemal tests turn positive as early as or earlier than the RPR, and she has no chancre.
w.Syphilis treated in the past: Treated syphilis leaves a treponemal test that stays positive for life with a falling RPR, the reverse of her reactive RPR and negative TP-PA.
w.Late latent syphilis: Latent syphilis has no signs but always keeps a reactive treponemal test, so a negative TP-PA excludes it at any stage of infection.
w.Prozone effect from high titer: The prozone effect occurs when huge antibody excess prevents flocculation, giving a falsely negative RPR in secondary syphilis, not a weakly reactive one.

bl: A reactive RPR with a negative treponemal test in lupus is a false positive from antiphospholipid antibodies binding cardiolipin.

pt.say: Read the bottom note: the nontreponemal test has false positives in lupus, because antiphospholipid antibodies bind cardiolipin while the treponemal test stays negative.

s: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 12 weeks' gestation has routine prenatal laboratory studies. Her RPR is reactive at a titer of 1:32, and a treponemal antibody test is positive. She has no rash or genital lesions and does not recall any. She has never been treated for syphilis. Ten years ago she developed hives, wheezing and hypotension after an injection of penicillin.
l: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Desensitize, then give benzathine penicillin G
Azithromycin as a single 2 g oral dose
e: A reactive RPR with a positive treponemal test in an untreated patient means syphilis, here latent syphilis of unknown duration, which is treated as late latent disease with three weekly doses of benzathine penicillin G. Treponemes cross the placenta, and only **penicillin** G reliably treats the fetus and prevents congenital syphilis. Her history of anaphylaxis therefore calls for **desensitization**, the stepwise introduction of the drug under monitoring, followed by full treatment. Doxycycline suits nonpregnant adults but harms fetal bones and teeth. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin have not been shown to protect the fetus, and azithromycin resistance is common.

w.Doxycycline twice daily for 28 days: Doxycycline treats latent syphilis in a nonpregnant adult allergic to penicillin, but tetracyclines stain teeth and impair fetal bone growth, and they are not proven to cure fetal infection.
w.Intramuscular ceftriaxone daily for 10 d: Ceftriaxone is active against treponemes, but its ability to treat the fetus is unproven, and cross-reactivity after anaphylaxis to penicillin remains a concern.
w.Azithromycin as a single 2 g oral dose: Macrolide-resistant strains of Treponema pallidum are widespread, and azithromycin does not reliably prevent congenital syphilis, so it is not used in pregnancy.
w.Postpone treatment until after delivery: Treponemes cross the placenta at any gestational age, so waiting risks stillbirth and congenital syphilis with bone, skin and neurologic damage.

et: Desensitize, then give benzathine penicillin G
Azithromycin as a single 2 g oral dose
bl: Syphilis in a penicillin-allergic pregnant patient requires desensitization and then benzathine penicillin G, the only drug proven to treat the fetus.

s: A 21-year-old woman comes for a routine health maintenance visit. She has had two male sexual partners in the past year and uses an oral contraceptive. She has no symptoms, and pelvic examination is normal. She has never been tested for sexually transmitted infections.
l: Which test should be offered to screen for chlamydia and gonorrhea?
o: Nucleic acid amplification test of a vaginal swab
Serum antibody titers for both organisms
Saline wet mount of vaginal discharge
e: Sexually active women younger than 25 years are screened every year for chlamydia and gonorrhea, because most cervical infections are asymptomatic yet can ascend and scar the tubes. The screening test is a **nucleic acid amplification** test, and a vaginal swab, which the patient can collect herself, is the preferred specimen because it is the most sensitive. Gram stain detects gonococci in men's urethral pus but misses most cervical infections, culture on Thayer-Martin agar is less sensitive and misses chlamydia entirely, serology plays no role, and a wet mount looks for trichomonads and clue cells.

w.Gram stain of endocervical secretions: Gram stain helps in symptomatic men with urethral discharge, but in the cervix it is insensitive for gonococci and cannot show chlamydia at all.
w.Serum antibody titers for both organisms: Antibodies to chlamydia and gonorrhea do not separate past from current infection, so they are not used to screen for or diagnose genital infection.
w.Endocervical culture on Thayer-Martin ag: Thayer-Martin culture grows gonococci and is kept for susceptibility testing, but it is less sensitive than amplification and cannot grow obligate intracellular chlamydiae.
w.Saline wet mount of vaginal discharge: A wet mount shows motile trichomonads or the clue cells of bacterial vaginosis; it cannot detect cervical chlamydia or gonorrhea.

et: Nucleic acid amplification test of a vaginal swab
Serum antibody titers for both organisms
Saline wet mount of vaginal discharge
bl: Sexually active women younger than 25 get yearly chlamydia and gonorrhea screening by nucleic acid amplification test of a vaginal swab.

s: A 25-year-old man comes to the clinic because of burning on urination and a scant, clear urethral discharge for 1 week. An urgent care physician prescribed cephalexin 5 days ago, but his symptoms have not changed. Temperature is 37°C. Gram stain of the discharge shows many neutrophils but no organisms, and culture on Thayer-Martin agar shows no growth. A urine nucleic acid amplification test is pending.
l: Which feature of the most likely organism explains why the cephalosporin failed?
o: Its cell wall has little peptidoglycan
It has a mutated penicillin-binding protein
It pumps beta-lactams out by efflux
It forms a biofilm on the urethra
e: Urethritis with neutrophils but no organisms on Gram stain and no gonococcal growth is nongonococcal urethritis, most often from *Chlamydia trachomatis*. Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular bacteria whose wall contains almost no **peptidoglycan**, the polymer that penicillin-binding proteins build and beta-lactams attack, so cephalexin has no target. Doxycycline, which blocks the bacterial ribosome, is the treatment. Beta-lactamase production and altered penicillin-binding proteins are how gonococci and other bacteria resist beta-lactams, but only in organisms that build a peptidoglycan wall. Efflux and biofilm are not why chlamydia ignores these drugs.

w.It produces a plasmid beta-lactamase: Plasmid beta-lactamases give gonococci penicillin resistance, but this organism did not grow on Thayer-Martin agar, and chlamydiae have no peptidoglycan target to protect.
w.It has a mutated penicillin-binding prot: Altered penicillin-binding proteins explain resistance in pneumococci, MRSA and some gonococci, organisms that still build a peptidoglycan wall for the drug to attack.
w.It pumps beta-lactams out by efflux: Efflux pumps add to multidrug resistance in gram-negative rods, but chlamydial resistance to cephalosporins is intrinsic, from lacking the target, not from exporting the drug.
w.It forms a biofilm on the urethra: Biofilms protect organisms on catheters and prosthetic valves; the chlamydial reticulate body instead hides and divides inside an epithelial inclusion.

et: Its cell wall has little peptidoglycan
It has a mutated penicillin-binding protein
It pumps beta-lactams out by efflux
It forms a biofilm on the urethra
bl: Chlamydia's cell wall has little peptidoglycan, so beta-lactams fail and nongonococcal urethritis is treated with doxycycline.

s: A 35-year-old man who recently returned from 6 months of work in southern Africa has a slowly enlarging genital lesion. Examination shows a painless, beefy-red ulcer with rolled edges that bleeds easily when touched, and no true lymphadenopathy. A crushed tissue smear stained with Giemsa shows dark, bipolar-staining bacteria inside the cytoplasm of macrophages.
l: Which organism is the most likely cause?
e: A painless, beefy-red, friable ulcer without true lymphadenopathy in someone from an endemic tropical region is **granuloma inguinale** (donovanosis), caused by *Klebsiella granulomatis*. The diagnostic finding is the Donovan body: encapsulated bacteria inside macrophages that stain dark and bipolar, like a safety pin, on Giemsa. Treatment is azithromycin for at least 3 weeks, until the ulcer heals. *Leishmania donovani* shares only the name; it causes visceral leishmaniasis with fever and splenomegaly. Haemophilus ducreyi causes painful ulcers, Treponema pallidum a clean indurated chancre, and serovar L2 chlamydia a fleeting ulcer followed by buboes.

w.Haemophilus ducreyi: Chancroid ulcers are painful with a purulent, ragged base and a suppurating node; the rods lie outside cells in school-of-fish chains, not within macrophages.
w.Treponema pallidum: The syphilis chancre is painless too, but it is clean-based and indurated rather than friable, and spirochetes appear on darkfield microscopy, not within macrophages.
w.Chlamydia trachomatis serovar L2: Lymphogranuloma venereum causes only a tiny transient ulcer and then painful inguinal buboes, the opposite of a large bleeding ulcer without true nodes.
w.Leishmania donovani: Leishmania donovani is a protozoan whose amastigotes fill macrophages in visceral leishmaniasis, causing fever, weight loss and massive splenomegaly, not a genital ulcer.

bl: A painless beefy-red ulcer with Donovan bodies in macrophages is donovanosis from Klebsiella granulomatis, treated with prolonged azithromycin.

pt.say: Look at the last row: Klebsiella granulomatis gives a beefy-red ulcer that bleeds on contact, no true nodes and Donovan bodies on Giemsa stain.
